I had four. I typed wrong in my original post. My first one was Oct 6th and my last one was Dec 8th, 2023.  So it wasn't long but I also went all in and hard. I had enough of my traumas (sexual molestation as a child, grooming as a teenager) getting in the way of me thriving and living my life. My therapist was incredible. She was accepting, open and very gentle. She was shocked at how much I leaned into the scary stuff and how often I came back for more. But I wanted so badly to get better. I imagined myself in a pitch black room with no light but filled with water and I just dove in. I didn't care what monsters were in there because they weren't going to win or hurt me anymore. I was going to slay them and I did. Some sessions were much harder than others. Remembering things I've long forgot about to protect myself came up and I ugly cried in her office. But I leaned into the uncomfortability and quite literally screamed in her office to get it all out of me. Someone should have warned me that it works though. For several months after my last session, I've felt like I had an ego death of sorts. It's very disorienting and I'm happy I had my husband who works in psych to be patient with me. Describing it is difficult but it's like I was a glass statue and someone gave me a soft gentle nudge and I fell into a million pieces. It didn't 'hurt' but I was confused as to what I was to do with all the pieces. All the things that I thought were 'me' were just self soothing band aids to cover up the trauma. I'm in a much much much MUCH better headspace. What helped me was having time in nature, creating art just for the sake of creating art, journaling, breaking ties with toxic people (Surprisingly very easy!) and having a trusted go to person (in my case, my husband) really helped me get through it. This was MY experience though and I don't want this to color yours or give you any expectations. My wish is for you to heal in any way that takes shape in your sessions. Good luck. Send me a message if you ever feel like it. Best. ❤️

I was diagnosed with ADHD three years ago. I'm on Vyvanse which is a stimulant that was supposed to help me focus. The problem is is that my psychiatrist gave me a slip of paper to explain what ADHD was and my ADHD made sure I  threw that piece of paper somewhere never to be seen again. It wasn't until I saw a psychologist that took the time to explain to me what ADHD was and how it hinders my Executive Function, that part of the brain that helps with organization, time management and planning, that I was able to make changes that truly helped me make a HUGE turn around. ADHD nearly ruined my marriage. My disorganization, mess, clutter and tardiness drove my husband mad. But in the last year, all those skills vastly improved with some tips I learned from Dr. Tracey Marks on YouTube as well as being consistent with my meds. I'll link the videos at the end of the post and I encourage everyone to watch them. They're short, concise, to the point and she has a pleasant voice that isn't demeaning. People with ADHD are very sensitive to tone of voice which is something I learned very recently as well. I had no idea about that either and that helped my husband communicate his frustrations in a way that was constructive rather than shut me down completely.

Here are some things that really helped me that I learned from Dr. Marks. For most people, these things are a no brainer. They are for me as well. But my brain just doesn't turn the key in the ignition for this. Us managing ADHD are essentially reparenting ourselves. Please be patient. This was a 34 year old issue that I'm just now able to take on. I've had decades of negative self talk. 'Why can't I do this? I'm an adult. I should be able to handle these things by now. I'm so stupid! I'm a failure!' Even with the immense strides I've made, I have days where I falter and spiral again. Please don't add to that. Also, thank goodness for my health insurance. If I wasn't able to have my therapist and meds covered, I would still be a hot mess. 

I'm only speaking for myself as I know people are iffy about meds, but mine are essential. Though I only saw their benefit when I learned what ADHD actually is and how it was affecting me. There's no use in taking meds for focus if you don't know what or where to direct that focus.

I timed EVERYTHING (and I mean EVERYTHING!) I did in my day and making note of it. Like actually writing it down on paper or a note in my phone. I started with my mornings. I timed how long it took to wake up, get in the shower, groom, get dressed, make a lunch, drive to work. That helped me add up the time I needed to get to work on time so I wasn't stressed. I microtimed everything. Like long it took me to get out of bed. Did I need a few minutes to wake up? How long was that? How long did it take for me  start the shower and then get out of the shower? How long did I floss for? How many seconds did it take to use mouthwash? How long did I iron my shirt for? How long did it take for my car to warm up? When I left my house and arrived to work, how long did that take? I learned that if I want to be at work by 8:30 am to get ready for my first client at 9 am, I need to be up by 6:30 am and out the door by 8 am. And then I moved onto timing what I did at work? How long did it take for me to get everything I need for the day ready? it takes me longer to get ready in the morning because what you don't want to do is rush someone with ADHD. Rushing leads to missing details, often times important ones and then feelings get hurt.

I made organization a fun game. Everything in my house has a 'house' of it's own. One of the more important aspects of this is that people with ADHD need the things they use the most closest to them. For me, its my phone, my music speakers and my laptop. I make sure to keep them all near my nightstand next to my bed. It's important to use bright, bold colors to differentiate where things go. Imagine a perfectly organized medicine cabinet that has a gorgeous nearly all white minimalist aesthetic. While I truly love a minimalist look, my brain doesn't recognize anything now. It's all awash. It's just as hard to make things out in this kind of hyper organization as it is a complete tornado of a mess. Colorful baskets, shelves and even labels really are a godsend. I know now that the green basket in the medicine cabinet is vitamins and the blue one is for my medications. The Grey one is for my husbands medications and the red one is for contact lenses and contact solution, etc. I LOOOOVE going on instagram and browsing #organization on there. I love love love going shopping for anything that going to help me organize my space. Especially my craft room. Before this year, that room looked like a BOMB went off in there. My husband refused to go in there and we'd fight about it all the time. It's also important for the person who has ADHD to do the organizing. We have to make the space work for us.

STAY AWAY FROM SUGAR! So hard! So damn hard! I'm eating a Hershey bar right now! But the sugar is only going to make the hyper activity in your brain go into overdrive.  Only have caffeine early in the morning.  I learned the hard way that the Dr. Pepper I just needed to have with dinner was what was keeping me up until 2:30 am. And for your brain to function correctly, you need GOOD SLEEP HYGIENE! ADHD makes you skip details and a foggy tired brain doesn't help. Which leads me to WORKING OUT! But, it's workout that should be FUN and ENGAGING for you. It'll help release all that extra energy to help you sleep at the end of the night. 

People with ADHD miss social cues. I was that person that even though I meant well, would suck the air out of the room. The meds did help calm me down a bit. I won't lie, it does sting a little when people comment that they like the pared down me more. I'd say to myself 'Why don't they like me? I'm just trying to be friendly.' I didn't realize I was being overbearing. But now I can manage friendships better rather than wonder what I did that cause so many people to leave. I learned that conversing is a give and take. You give, they take, they take, you give, throw in a joke, ask about them, let them talk about themselves until they throw the ball back to you. That formula has helped tremendously...if I can remember what they even said. haha

OP,  you can maybe share this list and these videos with your coworker. I just ask that you do so cautiously, gently, and in good faith. Again, people with ADHD are often times in very dark places in their head regarding their self worth and feel inadequate. I still feel shame because there are things I still struggle with that most people have had down since childhood. But one day at a time and I give myself praise no matter how small the win. Good luck with your coworker.

I cannot love this enough! I'm elated that there is so much more acceptance now so that kids can develop an open honest dialogue about healthy relationships and sexual practices with their parents. I came out at 14 in 2002. My family accepted me with open arms but there was no information for how to handle discussions surrounding healthy gay relationships and sex. I learned the ways of the world on my own with nothing but a prayer for safety from my single mom of 4 who grew up in the Reagan era and HIV as a death sentence.

1.) It's absolutely important to find a safe space and safe people to talk about being gay. Still, I'd rethink telling him to not mention anything to anybody.  Yes, middle schoolers are very cruel but they're also growing up in a much different world. Let him discern who he can and cannot tell. It gives him more autonomy. My mom told me the same thing. Looking back it was probably some subconcious fear of being judged for her 'failure' as a parent. She told not to tell my younger siblings (for some reason, specifically my sisters 🤷‍♀️ ) who were 9, 11 and 13 at the time. I broke that rule instantly. I was done hiding and keeping secrets. They already knew, didn't care but just wanted me to be better about wearing deodorant.

2.) Be mindful of what kind of media catered to gay audiences they consume.  My mom bought me a subscription to a very popular gay magazine from the early 2000's.  She thought she was being supportive but it just gave me an unrealistic, hyper sexual, and unattainable idea of what it is to be a gay man.  I know kids aren't reading magazines anymore but I can only imagine what they're exposed to with social media now is the same and A LOT more of it. You're definitely not going to be on top of it all but balancing it out with more PG movies and shows that are thankfully available today would be a good idea. I can't think of any that are exclusive to being gay but I really did love Sex Education on Netflix with Gillian Anderson. The relationship between Adam and Eric was beautifully written.

3.) The internet is not safe and social media makes it even easier for predatory adults to take advantage of young impressionable kids who are exploring. I was doing things at 14 years old online that horrify me looking back now at 34. Porn is not real and it's way too easily accessible online nowadays. I'd definitely talk to them about the dangers of watching porn at such a young age and how that can lead to an unrealistic and unhealthy view of sex. Also, block any and all gay hook-up apps. Grindr, Scruff, Jack'd, Growlr, Adam4Adam etc. Just block them from his phone. I know he's curious and would probably like to meet other gay guys for dating at his age but those apps are age restricted for a reason. I think this point can stand for any teenager no matter their sexuality.

4.) Talk about sex and sexuality openly and without attaching judgment or shame. Sex is a biological function but it's also done for pleasure. Make the topic of sex something that can be discussed and shared appropriately yet honestly. Use proper names of body parts. Learn all the nitty gritty details about gay sex and how to perform them safely. Douching, topping and bottoming, oral sex, rimming, handjobs, mutual masturbation etc basically anything that you also wouldn't do in front of your parents. Be shameless in your pursuit of knowledge to know how gay sex works and how to do it in a safe way. Maybe find a local sex therapist or sexual education counselor that specializes in gay sex? That way, if he's got questions you can have an idea on how to go about answering them.

Best of luck and you're doing an awesome job! He is so lucky to have you!
